title: Moment of Inertia of a Uniform Circular Disc
short_intro: The moment of inertia of a uniform circular disc quantifies its rotational inertia about a specified axis. For a standard disc of mass M and radius R, it depends strictly on the axis orientation relative to its geometrical plane and center.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Direct application of standard formulas for moment of inertia about central transverse axis (perpendicular to plane), parallel axis theorem, and perpendicular axis theorem.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation using mass element integration for arbitrary axes, integration of annular rings, and combined systems involving discs and rings.

prerequisites: Definition of moment of inertia I = int r<sup>2</sup> dm

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Meaning
bullets: Moment of inertia measures the rotational inertia of a rigid body about a rotational axis, analogous to inertial mass in translational motion.
For a continuous mass distribution, it is calculated as the sum of mass elements weighted by the square of their perpendicular distances from the axis.
The SI unit of moment of inertia is kg m<sup>2</sup> and its dimensional formula is [ML<sup>2</sup>T<sup>0</sup>].

concept_notes.heading: Moment of Inertia about Central Perpendicular Axis
bullets: For a uniform circular disc of mass M and radius R, the axis passes through the center of mass and is perpendicular to the plane of the disc.
The standard formula derived via annular element integration is I = \frac{1}{2} MR<sup>2</sup>.
All mass is distributed within the planar surface, resulting in a coefficient of 1/2 compared to 1 for a ring.

concept_notes.heading: Moment of Inertia about a Diameter
bullets: A diameter lies entirely in the plane of the disc and passes through the center.
By symmetry, two mutually perpendicular diametrical axes in the plane of the disc have equal moments of inertia (I<sub>x</sub> = I<sub>y</sub> = I<sub>diam</sub>).
Using the perpendicular axis theorem on the central perpendicular axis gives I<sub>diam</sub> = \frac{1}{4} MR<sup>2</sup>.

concept_notes.heading: Application of Parallel and Perpendicular Axis Theorems
bullets: The perpendicular axis theorem strictly applies to planar bodies (2D lamina) like a circular disc, relating the polar moment of inertia to two in-plane orthogonal diameters.

The parallel axis theorem is used to find the moment of inertia about an axis tangent to the edge in the plane (I = \frac{5}{4} MR<sup>2</sup>) or tangent perpendicular to the plane (I = \frac{3}{2} MR<sup>2</sup>).
These theorems allow extension from standard center-of-mass positions to any parallel or coplanar axis without repeating integration.

derivations.title: Moment of Inertia of a Disc about its Central Transverse Axis
derivations.conditions: Uniform disc of mass M, radius R, axis passing through center and perpendicular to plane.
steps: Define surface mass density sigma = \frac{M}{pi R<sup>2</sup>}.
Consider a concentric elementary ring of radius r and thickness dr. The mass of this ring is dm = sigma (2pi r dr) = \frac{2M}{R<sup>2</sup>} r dr.
The moment of inertia of this elementary ring about the central perpendicular axis is dI = r<sup>2</sup> dm = \frac{2M}{R<sup>2</sup>} r<sup>3</sup> dr.

Integrate dI from r = 0 to r = R to obtain the total moment of inertia: I = int_{0}^{R} \frac{2M}{R<sup>2</sup>} r<sup>3</sup> dr = \frac{2M}{R<sup>2</sup>} left[\frac{R<sup>4</sup>}{4}\right] = \frac{1}{2} MR<sup>2</sup>.

derivations.title: Moment of Inertia of a Disc about its Diameter
derivations.conditions: Uniform disc of mass M, radius R, using perpendicular axis theorem.
steps: Let the z-axis be perpendicular to the disc through the center, with moment of inertia I<sub>z</sub> = \frac{1}{2} MR<sup>2</sup>.
Let x and y be two mutually perpendicular diameters lying in the plane of the disc intersecting at the center.
By the perpendicular axis theorem for a planar body, I<sub>z</sub> = I<sub>x</sub> + I<sub>y</sub>.
Due to circular symmetry, I<sub>x</sub> = I<sub>y</sub> = I<sub>diam</sub>, which yields I<sub>z</sub> = 2 I<sub>diam</sub>.
Substitute I<sub>z</sub>: \frac{1}{2} MR<sup>2</sup> = 2 I<sub>diam</sub>, giving I<sub>diam</sub> = \frac{1}{4} MR<sup>2</sup>.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Torsional Pendulum Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A circular disc suspended by a vertical wire, showing torsional oscillation.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The time period T = 2pi sqrt{\frac{I}{C}} allows experimental determination of the moment of inertia I, where C is the torsional rigidity of the suspension wire.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually regarding factors affecting the time period of oscillation for a disc vs ring.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Moment of Inertia vs Mass (Constant Radius)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear graph of I versus M passing through the origin with slope R<sup>2</sup>/2.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows direct proportionality between moment of inertia and mass for a fixed geometrical radius.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting graphical slopes in objective questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Parallel Axis Verification Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic curve of I versus axis distance d starting from a minimum value I<sub>cm</sub> at d = 0.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the quadratic dependence I(d) = I<sub>cm</sub> + Md<sup>2</sup> as the axis is shifted away from the center of mass.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Identifying correct functional dependence in graphical MCQ items.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the moment of inertia of a uniform circular disc of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m about an axis passing through its center and perpendicular to its plane.
solution_steps: Identify the formula for a disc about its central perpendicular axis: I = \frac{1}{2} MR<sup>2</sup>.
Substitute the given values: M = 2 kg, R = 0.5 m.

solved_numericals.question: Find the moment of inertia of a circular disc of mass 4 kg and radius 1 m about any of its diameters.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for the moment of inertia of a disc about its diameter: I = \frac{1}{4} MR<sup>2</sup>.
Substitute M = 4 kg and R = 1 m.

solved_numericals.question: A uniform circular disc has mass M and radius R. Find its moment of inertia about an axis tangent to its edge and lying in the plane of the disc.
solution_steps: The axis is a tangent in the plane of the disc. The parallel axis theorem states I = I<sub>cm</sub> + Md<sup>2</sup>.
The moment of inertia about a diametrical axis through the center of mass is I<sub>cm</sub> = \frac{1}{4} MR<sup>2</sup>.
The distance between the diametrical axis and the tangent in the plane is d = R.
Substitute into the parallel axis theorem: I = \frac{1}{4} MR<sup>2</sup> + M(R)<sup>2</sup> = (\frac{1}{4} + 1) MR<sup>2</sup> = \frac{5}{4} MR<sup>2</sup>.

assumptions_and_limitations: The disc is assumed to be perfectly rigid, maintaining fixed relative positions of particles under rotation.
Mass distribution is strictly uniform, implying constant surface mass density (sigma = \text{constant}).
Effects of thickness are neglected (treated as a two-dimensional lamina), which introduces negligible error for thin discs but fails for thick cylinders.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Confusing the moment of inertia of a disc (\frac{1}{2} MR<sup>2</sup>) with that of a circular ring (\frac{1}{3} MR<sup>2</sup> or MR<sup>2</sup>).
common_misconceptions.correct: The moment of inertia of a ring is MR<sup>2</sup>, whereas for a disc it is \frac{1}{2} MR<sup>2</sup> due to mass distributed inward.
common_misconceptions.why: A ring has all its mass concentrated at distance R, while a disc has mass distributed from r = 0 to r = R.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Applying the perpendicular axis theorem to three-dimensional bodies like a solid sphere or cylinder.
common_misconceptions.correct: The perpendicular axis theorem is valid exclusively for two-dimensional planar bodies (laminas).
common_misconceptions.why: The theorem relies on I<sub>z</sub> = I<sub>x</sub> + I<sub>y</sub> where z is perpendicular to the xy plane containing the entire mass.

quick_revision: Central transverse axis of disc: I = \frac{1}{2} MR<sup>2</sup>.
Diametrical axis of disc: I = \frac{1}{4} MR<sup>2</sup>.
